finding.claim: Unauthenticated-to-note-existence oracle: a missing note ID returns HTTP 500 (KeyError) while an existing note the caller cannot access returns HTTP 403, so a client can tell whether a given note ID exists. Severity low; plausible.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled nid URL parameter on GET /n/<nid>, PUT /n/<nid>, and POST /n/<nid>/share.
finding.sink: Unchecked dictionary lookup NOTES[nid] that runs before any authorization check; the missing-key path raises KeyError (500) while the authorization path aborts with 403.

trace.note: read() route handler receives nid from the URL
n = NOTES[nid] raises KeyError for a nonexistent ID, which Flask returns as 500
require_view(g.user, n) runs only when the lookup succeeded
can_view checks owner or membership in shared
abort(403) returned for an existing note the caller cannot view
write() repeats the lookup before can_edit, same 500 vs 403 split
share() repeats the lookup before require_edit, same 500 vs 403 split

finding.guards_checked: Authorization checks (can_view/require_view, can_edit/require_edit) all run after the unguarded NOTES[nid] lookup, so they do not prevent existence disclosure. abort() raises, so no fall-through into the action. Note ID generation and the note-creation path are not in this file, so enumerability is unknown; if IDs are random UUIDs, exploitation is impractical but a leaked link still confirms existence. Fix would be NOTES.get(nid) with abort(404) before the authorization check.

verdict.guard_found: none. The only checks, require_view (notes.py:11-13), require_edit (notes.py:20-22) and the inline can_edit test in write() (notes.py:35-36), all run after the unguarded NOTES[nid] lookup at notes.py:27, :34 and :43. Nothing in the file catches a KeyError or returns 404 for a missing ID.
verdict.reason: For a nonexistent nid, NOTES[nid] at notes.py:27 raises KeyError before require_view at notes.py:28 runs, so Flask returns 500, while an existing note the caller cannot view hits abort(403) at notes.py:13, so the 500-vs-403 split discloses whether a note ID exists. The trace is accurate; the claim's "unauthenticated" wording is wrong, since g.user (used at notes.py:28, 35, 44) must be set by an auth layer outside this file, so the attacker is any authenticated low-privilege user. Severity is low, and exploitability depends on how note IDs are generated, which is not in this file.
